analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes false information about elections and government services and bans targeted online ads and data sales.
analysis.headline: A first-term bill with zero cosponsors sits in two House committees with no action, less than four months before the session ends.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create federal crimes for knowingly spreading false information about essential government services like voting, elections, public health, and the census, with up to five years in prison, and for widely amplifying messages encouraging violence. It would strip online platforms of their broad legal immunity when their algorithms target misinformation or violence at specific users or when they profit from it. It would also ban platforms from targeting advertisements at individuals using personal data, let users sue for $100-$5,000 per violation, and order the Federal Trade Commission to recommend limits on collecting and selling people's personal information [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users and voters. People would gain privacy protections against the collection and sale of their personal data, protection from political ads that follow them across the internet, and legal recourse against deliberate falsehoods designed to stop them from voting or accessing government services [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years, to knowingly spread false information about voting, elections, public health and safety, the census, civil rights, or education, with the intent that people act on it [S2].

Holds platforms criminally and civilly liable when they use algorithms and personal data to target fraudulent civic misinformation at selected users, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation [S2].

Narrows Section 230 immunity so platforms can be sued when they target content at specific individuals, act recklessly in spreading misinformation or violence, or run a business that profits from amplifying it [S2].
Bans targeted advertising on any online platform, and gives users a private right to sue for $100-$5,000 per violation, with pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for these claims [S2].

Directs the FTC to recommend legislation banning collection, aggregation, and sale of personal information without genuine, informed consent, including a finding that blanket consent-to-access deals do not count as consent [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large digital advertising platforms and data brokers, whose core business is collecting personal information and selling targeted ad delivery. Small businesses that rely on cheap targeted ads to reach customers would also bear costs, and news publishers and broadcasters are swept into the broad definition of a 'publishing entity' [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Digital ad platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Criminal penalties for spreading false information raise serious free-speech concerns; the bill's definitions of 'fraudulent civic misinformation' and 'publishing entity' are broad enough to cover newspapers and TV stations, and a future administration could enforce it selectively [S2].

A flat ban on targeted advertising would take away the main low-cost way small businesses reach potential customers online, and could push platforms toward paid subscriptions that limit access for lower-income users [S2].

Criminal liability for 'amplifying encouragement of violence' attaches at 500 viewers for individuals and 10,000 views for platforms, a threshold that could sweep in borderline political speech alongside genuine incitement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy and anti-targeting provisions would give ordinary users real protections they currently cannot get in the market, and the misinformation provisions aim at a genuine harm. But the criminal misinformation offense is drafted broadly enough that an honest supporter has to acknowledge the speech-chilling risk, and the ad-targeting ban is a blunt instrument that hits small advertisers along with the platforms. The bill is a strong statement of principle whose details would need substantial narrowing to survive court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in early September 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, where it has sat with no further action and no cosponsors as the session's remaining months run out [S1][S3][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. James McGovern (D-MA) introduced the Big Tech Accountability Act on September 4, 2026, with no cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction; no further action appears in the record [S4].
As of the latest record, no hearings, markups, or votes have been scheduled in either committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the online platforms and data brokers the bill targets, who remain untouched while the bill sits without a sponsor or cosponsor beyond its author.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Untouched ad platforms and data brokers

for.name: Rep. James P. McGovern
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been held and no one besides the Democratic sponsor signed on, so there is no record of how either party would line up.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms (social media, search, ad networks)
industries.note: A flat ban on targeted advertising strikes at the core revenue model of companies that collect personal data to sell individually targeted ads; the narrowed Section 230 immunity adds lawsuit exposure when their algorithms amplify misinformation or violence. Their interest in continuing the current model runs against the privacy and accuracy interests of users.

The bill directs the FTC to recommend prohibiting the collection, aggregation, and sale of personal information without genuine consent, threatening the broker business of trading in people's browsing data.

A targeted-ad ban removes the cheap, precise way small businesses find customers online, though their customers would regain privacy. The gain and loss here fall on opposite sides of the same transaction.

The bill's 'publishing entity' definition includes print publishers and broadcast licensees, exposing them to criminal and civil liability for disseminating fraudulent civic misinformation, while the Section 230 changes do not directly affect their own liability shield because they never had one.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action since its early-September referral, and only a few months left before the session ends January 3, 2027, the bill is all but certain to die without a vote, as most first-term bills referred to two committees do.
